text: What is the **contrapositive** of “if it rains, then the match is cancelled”?

options.t: If the match is cancelled, then it rains.
If it does not rain, then the match is not cancelled.
If the match is not cancelled, then it does not rain.
It rains and the match is not cancelled.

solution: Write the statement as $r \to c$ with $r$: it rains, $c$: the match is cancelled.
The contrapositive swaps the two sides **and** negates both: $\neg c \to \neg r$.
In words: if the match is not cancelled, then it does not rain. It is equivalent to the original.
concept: Contrapositive = swap and negate; it is the only variant equivalent to the original.

common_wrong.why: That only swaps the sides: it is the **converse** $c \to r$.
That only negates the sides: it is the **inverse** $\neg r \to \neg c$.
$r \wedge \neg c$ is the **negation** of the statement, the one situation it forbids.

text: On how many of the 8 rows of its truth table is $(p \vee q) \to r$ **false**?
solution: An implication is false exactly when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false.
So we need $p \vee q$ = T and $r$ = F.
$p \vee q$ is true for 3 of the 4 settings of $(p, q)$ (all but FF), and $r$ must be F: $3 \times 1 = 3$ rows.
concept: Count the false rows of an implication as (rows with a true hypothesis) × (rows with a false conclusion).

common_wrong.why: Counting only the row $p = q = $ T: $p \vee q$ is inclusive, so TF and FT also make it true.
5 is the number of rows where the implication is **true** ($8 - 3$); the question asks for the false rows.

text: Let $e$: “you can enrol” and $f$: “you have paid the fee”. Which formula represents “you can enrol **only if** you have paid the fee”?
solution: “$p$ only if $q$” is $p \to q$: $p$ cannot happen without $q$.
Here $p = e$ and $q = f$, so the sentence is $e \to f$.
Check by the forbidden situation: the sentence forbids enrolling without having paid, $e \wedge \neg f$, which is exactly the false row of $e \to f$.
concept: “p only if q” is p → q; the condition after “only if” is the conclusion.

common_wrong.why: $f \to e$ is “you can enrol **if** you have paid”, the converse.
$\neg e \to \neg f$ is the inverse of the sentence, equivalent to $f \to e$, the converse again.
The sentence promises nothing in the other direction: paying need not let you enrol.

solution: “Unless” means “if not”: “$q$ unless $p$” is “if not $p$, then $q$”.
So the formula is $\neg p \to q$, which is equivalent to $p \vee q$.
It forbids only the situation where $p$ fails and $q$ fails too.

eg p \wedge

$\neg q \to \neg p$ is the contrapositive of $p \to q$, so it is wrong for the same reason.
$q \to \neg p$ reads “$q$ only if not $p$”, a different claim.

text: On how many of the 8 assignments to $p, q, r$ do $p \to (q \to r)$ and $(p \to q) \to r$ take **different** truth values?
solution: $p \to (q \to r)$ is false only when $p$ = T, $q$ = T, $r$ = F (one row).
$(p \to q) \to r$ is false when $p \to q$ is T and $r$ is F: $(p, q) \in \{$TT, FT, FF$\}$ with $r$ = F (three rows).
They differ on the rows where exactly one is false: FTF and FFF.
So they differ on **2** rows; implication is not associative.
concept: → is right-associative and not associative; compare the false rows of the two groupings.

common_wrong.why: Treating → as associative. On $p = q = r = $ F the first is T (false hypothesis) and the second is F.
That is the number of false rows of $(p \to q) \to r$; one of them (TTF) is also false for the other grouping.

concept: Rewrite an operator from its false row (here NAND), then substitute each option.

common_wrong.why: Negating a NAND gives AND, not OR.
$p \ast (q \ast q) = p \ast \neg q = \neg p \vee q$, which is $p \to q$.
$p \ast q$ is the NAND itself, false only on TT.

text: It is known that $p \to q$ is **false**. What is the truth value of $(q \to r) \wedge (r \vee \neg p)$?
solution: $p \to q$ is false only when $p$ = T and $q$ = F. Nothing is known about $r$.
$q \to r = $ F $\to r$ = T whatever $r$ is.
$r \vee \neg p = r \vee $ F $= r$.
So the formula equals $r$: true if $r$ is true, false otherwise. It cannot be determined.
concept: A false implication fixes both its parts (p = T, q = F); evaluate the rest and see what is still free.

common_wrong.why: $q \to r$ is indeed true, but the second conjunct is just $r$, which is unknown.
$q$ is already known to be F, so this would make the formula always false; in fact it depends on $r$.

text: Which of the following say the same thing as “$x$ being even is **necessary** for $x$ to be divisible by 4”?

options.t: If $x$ is divisible by 4, then $x$ is even.
$x$ is even only if $x$ is divisible by 4.
$x$ is divisible by 4 only if $x$ is even.
If $x$ is not even, then $x$ is not divisible by 4.

solution: “$a$ is necessary for $b$” is $b \to a$. With $a$: $x$ even, $b$: $x$ divisible by 4, the sentence is $b \to a$.
(A) is $b \to a$. Same.
(B) is $a \to b$ (“$a$ only if $b$”), the converse. Different.
(C) is $b \to a$. Same.
(D) is $\neg a \to \neg b$, the contrapositive of $b \to a$. Same.
concept: The necessary condition is the conclusion; “p only if q” and the contrapositive say the same.

common_wrong.why: (B) reverses the direction: being even does not force divisibility by 4 ($x = 6$).
(D) is the contrapositive of (A), so it is equivalent.

text: How many assignments of truth values to $p, q, r, s$ make **exactly two** of the four variables true **and** make $p \to q$ true?
solution: Exactly two true: choose the true pair, $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ assignments.
$p \to q$ is false only when $p$ = T and $q$ = F. Among the pairs, those containing $p$ but not $q$ are $\{p, r\}$ and $\{p, s\}$.
Remove them: $6 - 2 = 4$ assignments ($\{p, q\}, \{q, r\}, \{q, s\}, \{r, s\}$).
concept: Count by complement: all rows meeting the count condition minus those on the implication's false row.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting the second condition: two of the pairs put $p$ = T, $q$ = F.
Removing $\{p, q\}$ as well: there $p \to q$ = T → T = T, so it stays.
